<title>Thanksgiving dinner is likely to be served with a side of political disagreement</title>

Clendenin/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Every year as Thanksgiving approaches, news stories are written about how holiday gatherings bring together people who see the world very differently, sometimes <a href="https://www.news-press.com/story/opinion/2026/11/07/navigating-uncomfortable-thanksgiving-conversations-opinion/92618504007/">leading to uncomfortable dinner conversations</a>. <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/life/health-wellness/how-to-handle-your-stressful-family-at-thanksgiving/92223489007/">The stories usually include advice</a> about avoiding awkward moments and topics that are off-limits, and navigating heated conversations if they arise.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1468-0009.12040">experts in health communication</a> and public health, we are keenly aware of how conversations with family members and close friends <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10410236.2022.2114768">shape people’s decisions and actions</a> and that sometimes the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/00909882.2013.781659">benefits of having difficult conversations</a> outweigh the potential costs. We wondered how often difficult conversations actually take place at Thanksgiving meals and what the conversations are about. </p>

<p>Although studies have demonstrated that Thanksgiving meals involving people with diverse political viewpoints were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0239988">shorter by 24 minutes</a> than meals among people holding similar views, we found no estimates of how often these conversations occur.</p>

<p>Our survey of 354 adults from 17 states found that over half – 57% – will share a Thanksgiving meal this year with at least one person from outside their household who sees the world very differently than they do. In 4 out of 5 of these cases, the way their viewpoints differ is politics. </p>

<p>The survey participants were initially recruited to represent differing perspectives on health; they were not randomly selected to represent the general population. That means the survey’s findings may not be generalizable beyond the study sample.  </p>



<h2>Table talk: What do Americans expect this Thanksgiving?</h2>

<p>From Nov. 7-9, 2026, we surveyed 354 adults from 17 states about their plans for this year’s Thanksgiving. Respondents were part of an ongoing <a href="https://hcrl.wustl.edu/iheard-usa/">health knowledge monitoring and response system</a>. Their mean age was 47.1 years; three-quarters of them were women; and they were racially and ethnically diverse, with 44% white, 33% African American, 15% Hispanic ethnicity and 8% another race or ethnicity. About 1 in 10 were rural residents, and 43% had children under 18 living in their home.</p>

<p>The questions about Thanksgiving meals were sent to 430 people on Nov. 7; 354 completed a survey, which is an 82% response rate. </p>

<p>Of the 354 respondents, 80% expected to share a meal with family members or friends from outside their household during the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday. </p>

<p><iframe id="n99gy" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/n99gy/3/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="People expect to encounter different views at Thanksgiving."></iframe></p>

<p>Those planning to share a meal with others from outside their household were then asked, “Holiday meals sometimes bring together people from different generations, with different views, or different life experiences. Thinking about your upcoming Thanksgiving meal, will anyone be there who sees the world very differently than you do?” </p>

<p>Almost 71% of those planning to share a meal with others outside their household said yes.</p>

<p>Asked “What are those differences about?” by far the most common response was politics, at 81%, followed by religion at almost 58%, differing views about people such as their career choices or relationships at 54%, health at 53%; and half of the respondents said money. A few mentioned other differences such as “raising children” and “parenting” and “gender expression” and “LGBTQ.”</p>

<p>Asked if they think any of those differences will be expressed during the meal, almost 60% said yes. This was especially true for differences in politics. A large majority – 79% – of respondents said that differences in politics would be expressed during the meal. Fewer respondents – 40% or less – expected that differences in views about people, money, religion or health would be expressed. </p>

<p>Then our questions got to who is expected to disagree – and what respondents anticipate the disagreements will be about. These responses varied by race and ethnicity.  </p>

<p>White respondents were more likely than African American or Hispanic respondents to say that others at their Thanksgiving meal will view politics differently from them. African American respondents were more likely than White or Hispanic respondents to say that others at their meal will view money matters differently and were more likely than Hispanics to say that others at their meal will view certain people differently.</p>

<p><iframe id="a8poZ" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/a8poZ/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Diverse views are coming to Americans' holidays"></iframe></p>

<p>In short, it’s highly common for those gathered around any Thanksgiving table this year to have different views on key matters, but the differences you’re most likely to hear about during mealtime conversation are political.</p>

<h2>The value in disagreeing</h2>

<p>Science tells us that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2012.02.017">conflict resolution improves through dialogue</a> by <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2023.101696">reducing stereotypes and changing attitudes</a> that tend to divide people. Holiday meals could provide some clues about how Americans navigate conversations with those who hold different viewpoints from them on politics, religion, money and health. </p>

<p>As one panel member commented: “I don’t keep people around just because they agree with me on something. I don’t cut people away because we disagree about something.”</p>

title: Jensen Huang and the Myth of Indispensability
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Jensen Huang said in a statement this morning that he would be “honored” to return to Nvidia, the computer-chip giant from which he was ousted just last week
Unfortunately for Huang, the company’s board made it clear on today’s earnings call that it’s not considering rehiring him
But major figures in Silicon Valley have been making a show of their continued support

For another, less powerful executive, reports of extramarital affairs with three women —one of whom is alleged to be a Chinese spy and another of whom was a direct subordinate—would likely be seen as irredeemable lapses in judgment

Yet Huang’s endorsers don’t seem to view this as the end of his career at the company. “Without Jensen,” Elon Musk claimed on X this weekend, Nvidia will lose important “handshake” deals that Huang personally negotiated
Gavin Baker, whose firm invests in Nvidia, has written that he’s in favor of reinstating Huang as the investigations play out

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney remarked on X that “journalists with sketchy motives” effectively “gaslit” the board into pushing out a “once-in-generation visionary.” An Uber co-founder, Travis Kalanick, who knows a thing or two about tech ousters , was among the more than 195,000 signatories of a petition to reinstate Huang as the company’s CEO—as were Musk, Baker, and Sweeney
The Wall Street Journal reports that a high-level Nvidia employee sent a letter to the company’s board warning that “irreplaceable talent” might leave if Huang isn’t reinstated

When President Trump was asked yesterday whether he’d support the return of Huang, a close ally, he told reporters, “I would not mind that.” Ultimately, none of these people has full control over Huang’s fate
That power belongs to Nvidia’s board of directors

But the support for Huang, despite his clearly disqualifying transgressions, is a testament to the power that this one man has held over Nvidia and the economy at large. (It may also be informed by the dramatic firing and rehiring of another tech titan: Sam Altman.) Even though Huang is accused of having jeopardized national security, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is now reportedly probing whether Nvidia violated investor-disclosure laws, his backers insist that he remains indispensable
Their argument is that he is the company, and that the risks of losing him might actually outweigh the risks of bringing him back as CEO
In a way, they are right: Huang has made himself synonymous with Nvidia
But his centrality is a liability rather than an asset
This moment should be a reckoning about the risks of relying so heavily on any one CEO—yet many in the industry are reinforcing the opposite lesson, doubling down on a disgraced executive
Nvidia is what you might call a “systematically important” institution—industry lingo for a company whose failure would destabilize parts of the financial system
Wall Street trembled after the revelations about Huang spurred a roughly $1.5 trillion sell-off in Nvidia stock (equivalent to more than 25 percent of the company’s value)

The AI sector, and in turn the entire U.S. economy, is heavily dependent on the firm’s chips. “Nvidia has much of the financial system in a hostage situation,” my colleague Charlie Warzel wrote last week. “Huang is too big to fail

Which may be why so many people seem motivated to downplay or protect him right now.” Some of this is owed to the myth of the tech leader as an irreplaceable genius—a story that Silicon Valley loves to tell
As The Washington Post points out , nearly a tenth of the value of the S&P 500 is tied to companies with no clear successor: Nvidia, Tesla, and Meta
Huang himself liked to boast about his famously flat org structure—he had 60 direct reports
The New York Times notes that Nvidia’s board, which is now investigating whether Huang was the target of Chinese espionage, has a history of “loyalty and deference” to him
Some of its directors have been on the board since 1993

Public outcry has been an effective tactic in bringing back ousted tech leaders in the past; in late 2023, OpenAI’s board fired Altman because he “was not consistently candid in his communications” with them—but reinstated him five days later after a company-wide revolt
Like Huang, Altman is a celebrity co-founder
He’s the face of his company and the person seen as largely responsible for its success
Any of Altman’s shortcomings or misdeeds were considered secondary to, and distinct from, his ability to generate value for shareholders

Obviously, this isn’t the first case of an executive facing consequences over a relationship with an employee: McDonald’s fired its CEO over this in 2019, Intel’s CEO resigned in 2018 after failing to disclose a relationship with a subordinate, Boeing pushed out its CEO in 2006 over a similar situation
The ongoing national-security concerns add another layer of urgency to the situation
The question of how much Huang actually knew about Megaspeed—the company that the alleged Chinese spy worked for, which the U.S
Department of Commerce has been looking into since 2024—is currently under investigation

Investors are angry enough that they’re suing Nvidia over the fiasco (the company had initially denied that there was anything “unusual or unexpected” about its CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive until Huang himself admitted to it; Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment)
Not everyone is pushing for Huang’s comeback
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has suggested that he’d like to see Nvidia pick a new CEO from outside the company, and some lawmakers have opposed the idea of Huang’s return
But those who want him reinstated are selling a dangerous narrative about the indispensability of any one leader

The celebrity investor Balaji Srinivasan wrote today that “it’s arguably a matter of US national security to immediately return the most important person in AI to his role at the top AI company”—never mind that Nvidia, under Huang, may have been responsible for allowing the United States’ biggest economic rival to access top-tier computer chips
Tying an entire enterprise to the success or failure of a single person comes with extreme risks; Huang’s defenders are ignoring them

title: Diplomacy, but Make It Obnoxious
excerpt: Tyra Banks had a tip for how contestants on America’s Next Top Model should present themselves: “Ho, but make it fashion.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s rece
body: Tyra Banks had a tip for how contestants on America’s Next Top Model should present themselves: “Ho, but make it fashion.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s recent speeches update the message with a twist: “Traditional American foreign policy, but make it obnoxious.” Twice in six weeks, Rubio has delivered addresses filled with classic conservative beliefs, but seasoned with the kind of racism, sexism, and enthusiasm for lawless power that has become common in the age of Trump

At a Federalist Society conference Friday evening, Rubio offered an explanation for the Trump administration’s decision last month to impose sanctions on what he called the “fake” International Criminal Court—a move apparently made in retaliation against the ICC’s investigation of alleged U.S. war crimes in Afghanistan
In making his case, Rubio had two options
The first would have been to point out that every American administration of the past three decades has rejected ICC jurisdiction over U.S. personnel
As president, Bill Clinton, Barack Obama , and Joe Biden all expressed openness to the ICC—but only if the court accepted some kind of U.S. veto
The case for this option is that it would have created the broadest possible coalition behind the Trump administration’s position
Bush’s administration took in the early 2000s, citing Clinton’s qualms about the ICC to support Bush’s stronger stance against the court
The second option was for Rubio to deliver a message of skepticism about the ICC, but going pedal-to-the-metal culture war
This, unfortunately, was the option Rubio went for

In explaining the administration’s policy toward the ICC, Rubio cited a line attributed to the Roman general Pompey: “Stop quoting laws to men with swords.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth liked the bit so much, he reposted it on X , capping “MEN WITH SWORDS.” [ Read: The dangerous idea Rubio and Hegseth are endorsing ] Watch the video of these remarks, and you’ll hear nervous laughter after Rubio’s Pompey reference

When he noticed that his big applause line had misfired, Rubio flashed an apologetic smile and improvised: “Not politically correct to say that, but that’s what he said!” The attempted regroup extracted more chuckles but scant applause
Rubio was speaking to an ultra-friendly room

The majority of the conservative lawyers convened before him surely agreed with his preceding point about the ICC: “They think they have the right to rule over everyone, but they are accountable to no one, armed with the power to investigate, to prosecute, to persecute, and to jail our citizens according to laws we neither consent nor control.” But American lawyers—even conservative ones—will not agree that the capacity to do violence exempts armed men from the law
We know Pompey’s views on men with swords because they appear in Plutarch’s collection of short biographies of eminent Greeks and Romans
Plutarch’s Pompey is no hero, but a man of great gifts laid low by bad judgment
After the Bible, Plutarch’s Lives ranked high among the books read by America’s Founding Fathers

James Madison, the country’s fourth president and Rubio’s predecessor as secretary of state by more than 215 years, had little good to say about warlords such as Pompey: “The liberties of Rome proved the final victim to her military triumphs.” Rubio has a reputation as one of the Trump’s administration’s less irresponsible figures
But his approach to rhetoric lately seems borrowed from a story told about Franklin D
During the presidential campaign of 1932, Moley showed Roosevelt two competing drafts of a big economic speech
Which approach, Moley asked, would the candidate prefer? “Weave the two together,” Roosevelt replied
Rubio likewise sometimes presents himself as the last voice of Republican internationalism, a defender of America’s long history of democratic alliances and partnerships
Other times, he remembers that this music no longer moves his party under Trump—and instead deploys language that is bombastic, vituperative, and needlessly disparaging

In Rubio’s speech on democracy in Athens last month, for example, he swerved from praising the pursuit of knowledge to delivering an encomium to violent conquest: “The hunger for new knowledge, that’s what gave birth to Magellan’s first expedition around the world, to Columbus’s discovery of the Americas, and ultimately to Apollo 11’s journey to the moon

And the qualities that led Alexander to conquer the entire known world reappeared in Caesar, then Charlemagne, and Cortes.” Rubio’s Federalist Society speech was mostly about international law, but it included a completely unnecessary passage that implied that Native Americans are not part of the American “we.” He said, “When our predecessors first arrived in North America, when they first came, there were no factories, there were no railroads, there were no skyscrapers
These things exist because we built them, because we acted

These things exist because we acted without fear or moral doubt and overcame all that which threatened or stood in our way.” [ Read: Trump sets the olive branch on fire ] These speeches deploy gendered language (“the men who founded my country”; “the men who built backwater colonies into the greatest superpower on Earth”; “the men who made the Parthenon”; “the sons of Athens and Rome”) with an emphasis and frequency that must have raised eyebrows even in a Trump-administration communications department

When I wrote speeches for a Republican administration more than a quarter century ago, language that obliviously elided about half of the human race would have earned me a zinger from one of the administration’s many high-ranking women

For the Cabinet secretary charged with the care of alliances and institutions, such fretting over the mollycoddling do-gooders who are crushing the spirits of the Nietzschean supermen among us is unusual

But in his speech in Greece, Rubio lamented that Western institutions care more for “the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best,” adding: “We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre.” To the Federalist Society, Rubio complained of how “international lawyers and jurists and NGOs and UN bureaucrats” conspire to persuade the United States “to relinquish responsibility for our own destiny and to relieve ourselves of the burdens of greatness and seek refuge in these glittering generalities of international law.” He expressed annoyance that the president “cannot restrict trade or immigration or even examine the way in which we spend our citizens’ tax dollars abroad without facing the fury” of these meddlesome international bodies: “Even as we defeated the institution of Soviet communism, we did not triumph over the spirit of Marx.” But it was not Karl Marx who struck down Trump’s attempts to exert unilateral presidential authority over trade and immigration

It was America’s own courts—in many cases led by Federalist Society–style judges—that ruled against Trump’s claims that the president can impose tariffs at will and overturn birthright citizenship by executive order

What’s achieved by these bizarre excursions down such malign byways? The early bidding for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination is shaping up as a contest among Vice President Vance, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, and a widening field that includes Rubio and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas
Like Vance, Rubio has seemed to intuit that the way to prove one’s mettle in a party remade by Trump is to present oneself as gratuitously nasty
But this is an odd gamble at a time when the president’s own gratuitous nastiness has inspired the country’s turn away from him and his party.

title: An Obituary for America’s Measles-Elimination Status
excerpt: UNITED STATES—A scientific triumph that quietly shaped a generation, the United States’ measles-elimination status passed away on Tuesday, November 17, 2026
body: UNITED STATES—A scientific triumph that quietly shaped a generation, the United States’ measles-elimination status passed away on Tuesday, November 17, 2026
Hailed as an unmitigated good and a borderline miracle on its initial appearance, then quickly forgotten, Measles Elimination had seemed to have many more good years ahead of it
Its decline was sudden and dramatic, and it had been feuding with the secretary of health and human services for some time, although he denied having any direct role in its demise

Observers described its death as “senseless,” “utterly senseless,” “an enormous step backward,” and “the kind of thing that makes you lose all hope in human progress.” Measles Elimination arrived in 2000 as the proud work of scientists and doctors and public messaging

Praised at the time as one of the country’s greatest public-health achievements, it had hoped to make way for many more such eliminations. “Now, instead, we are looking at the first of many obituaries that didn’t need to be written,” one observer commented

Parents are finding it wrenching to explain to their children that Measles Elimination won’t be around anymore. “I feel so bad that we took the elimination of measles for granted,” one mother said. “We were presenting it to our kids like, Measles Elimination isn’t going anywhere
Measles Elimination will be there long after I’m gone

No part of this is how I hoped I’d be explaining death to them for the first time.” “Measles Elimination never wanted to be the story,” its old friend and mentor Uncontaminated Food remarked. “It wanted the story to be the other things that it was making possible

I was always telling people: If you’re here, if you’re pursuing your dreams, if your immune system is functioning, if you’re attending school year-round without interruption, you owe that to Measles Elimination
People forgot all the work it was doing.” Uncontaminated Food coughed for an uncomfortably long period of time. “I always thought I would be the first to go
This makes me sick.” No ceremony will be held; Measles Elimination stated in its will that the last thing it would want would be a large gathering in its honor
It asked for donations to be made in its name to vaccine clinics
Measles Elimination was only 26—older, though, than many will get to be without it.

title: Trump’s Arch Must Be Stopped
excerpt: In 1962, my father faced a novel threat to the Constitution
body: In 1962, my father faced a novel threat to the Constitution
The governor of Mississippi had defied a federal court order and physically blocked a young Black Air Force veteran from attending the University of Mississippi
As U.S. attorney general, my father—Robert F
The governor was backed by a state police force that acted as his personal militia
There was, and is, no federal police force that my father or his brother, President John F
Kennedy, could deploy to deal with a lawless chief executive at the state level
My father cobbled together a force of duly deputized U.S. marshals, many of them drawn from the ranks of the U.S
He sent two courageous Justice Department attorneys—World War II veterans—to prepare the marshals before deploying them to Oxford, Mississippi
They were able, barely, to protect James Meredith on his first day at the university
Eventually, about 30,000 troops and National Guardsmen were activated to protect Meredith
The lesson my father drew was simple: The Constitution does not enforce itself
When those sworn to uphold the law refuse to do so, someone has to find a way with the tools at hand
Instead of a miscreant governor, the United States now has an unrepentant chief executive who treats the Department of Justice as his personal force
In 1962, the federal government would send marshals to Oxford

Today, when the lawbreaker is the commander in chief, the work falls to citizens: lawyers, nonprofits, preservation groups, and ordinary Americans who have taken this government to court again and again

Nine members of my family—seven children and one grandchild of Robert Kennedy and one son of the late Senator Ted Kennedy—are seeking to join the litigation to stop construction of the triumphal arch that Donald Trump wants to build near Arlington National Cemetery, a sacred space for military veterans and their loved ones
The plaintiffs in the ongoing lawsuit include veterans, an architectural historian, the District of Columbia, and the Commonwealth of Virginia

By building a gigantic memorial to himself, Trump would dishonor those who sacrificed themselves for this country. (His administration has claimed, variously, that the arch would honor the country’s 250th birthday, celebrate the troops, and serve as a military facility with snipers and drones.) The arch, modeled after the Arc de Triomphe, would be 250 feet high, more than double the height of every memorial in the capital except for the Washington Monument

Planned for a traffic circle next to the Potomac River, it would obstruct the view between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery that Congress has protected for generations of Americans
An eternal flame, which has burned for more than 60 years at President Kennedy’s grave, is bright enough to be seen by visitors at the Lincoln Memorial, but that too would be blocked
In the early morning, our parents’ resting place would lie in the shadow of the overbearing arch, as would many more graves
We should not allow this vanity to veil the sacrifice of the more than 400,000 men and women buried at Arlington
It violates two federal statutes: the Commemorative Works Act, which details a process for creating new memorials in D.C., as well as Title 40 of the U.S
Code, Section 8106, the law that forbids construction of any building or structure on federal reservations in Washington without the approval of Congress
The only path open to us in attempting to rein in the president is the courts

That is why, after reading an article that illustrates how the arch would cast shadows deep into the cemetery, we decided to seek to intervene in the litigation against Trump and the National Park Service
My mother liked to visit our father’s grave early in the morning, before going to Mass
She would head out of the house just after sunrise and drive herself down George Washington Memorial Parkway
Most of the guards came to know her white Oldsmobile by sight and would wave her through
She took great care in placing a simple wooden cross to mark his grave, and rough paving stones that reminded them both of the seaside streets of New England
She selected these words by my father to be cut into a granite block behind the grave: It is from numberless diverse acts of courage and belief that human history is shaped

Each time a man stands up for an ideal, or acts to improve the lot of others, or strikes out against injustice, he sends forth a tiny ripple of hope, and crossing each other from a million different centers of energy and daring those ripples build a current that can sweep down the mightiest walls of oppression and resistance
My mother passed away two years ago and is now buried beside her husband
People visiting their shared gravesite can read that quote and then, as I have done often, look up over the granite and down a hill once owned by Robert E
They can see Arlington Memorial Bridge leading to the Lincoln Memorial, where Dr
Martin Luther King Jr. addressed the crowds of the March on Washington
Their eyes can then trace the Reflecting Pool, the National Mall, the U.S
Capitol, and, finally, beyond that, the long-neglected neighborhoods on the southeast side of Washington, framed by the old site of RFK Stadium
Arlington Memorial Bridge symbolized the rejoining of North and South after the Civil War
Each side faces the other across an unbroken line of sight

title: Long Wave
excerpt: R uth sets the children to dig for coins under the cushions of the ratty green sofa while she tries to get enough swimsuits and towels together
body: R uth sets the children to dig for coins under the cushions of the ratty green sofa while she tries to get enough swimsuits and towels together
There is a big chest of drawers JP dragged home gleefully one evening, the scraping sound of her approaching, hollering for help
One of the other women, Sally, took it out into the concrete yard and sanded it down, repainted it, and then stenciled red flowers around the edges
As the women chopped carrots and argued about the rota, the children sneaked out at dusk and stuck their hands in the paint pot, left prints all over the front of the drawers

They get kids’ clothes from boxes on the street, charity sales and donations, and none of them fit right or they give way almost immediately at the seams but get shoved, nonetheless, into the chest of drawers and tugged out at random to put on whichever child needs them
Ori likes to go in by herself and dig thoughtfully through, chucking rejected dungarees and tie‑dye T‑shirts over her shoulder, plopping down on her backside to wrangle on leggings
Most of the swimsuits are nearly see-through from washing, the straps snapped, but Ruth manages to find enough and takes a handful of towels off the banister, puts them into the bag
The sun cream is out of date but will do the job
When she gets back into the sitting room, the cushions have been heaved off the sofa and everyone is bouncing on the wheezing springs
They have uncovered crushed breadsticks and molding apple cores but also a handful of lost 20-pence pieces, just enough for them all to get into the lido if she lies about some of their ages
She has been working all week, but today she is in charge
Ori rushes over and burbles something about jumping as high as the trees like a bird—no, like a dragon—and then tugs a pirate hat down as far as it will fit onto Ruth’s head
Let’s go, let’s go, she shouts, and everyone gathers, grabbing at shoes

There is Ori, who is 3—dressed this morning in a rainbow unicorn outfit with a wilting horn and a grubby tail—and Nora, with her shoes on the wrong feet, and Leo, who is 9 and an expert at making mayonnaise-and‑cheese sandwiches and wrapping them in foil
Last time they went to the lido he stole a rubber ring and he wears it slung around his middle now, hitching it up with one hand when it slithers down to his knees

There is also Bee, who is nearly 2 and who Ruth puts up on her hip to get out the door, and Tsembi, who is 7 and has a younger brother, Douglas, who bends to shit in his nappy beside the step, grunting intently
Sally has been making planters out of pallets to try to make some more money and they are stacked up outside the house with for sale signs pinned to them
Ruth and the kids make it down to the path and go in a ragtag, snaky line away from the house, Ruth yelling hold hands, hold hands, until everyone is pinned to someone else and trailing along
Ruth hitches Bee onto her shoulders and Leo and Tsembi take turns carrying Douglas
She changes Douglas’s nappy while the others climb onto the back of a bus-stop bench and compare war wounds
Douglas’s shit is runny and filled with little white worms again
It won’t be long before the others get them too
Ori is yelling loudly about being the fastest, fastest, fastest one and twisting back and forth to show off her scrapes and bumps, her multiple Moomin Band-Aids, which are grubby and starting to peel

Leo is hanging near her, his fingers beginning to tap a little in the way they do when everything is too loud and busy, his eyes glazing; Ruth calls him closer, tries to distract him, asks him to pass her cloths and then take the dirty nappy to a bin
Nora and Ori are arguing about who can stand on the back of the bench the longest without holding on
Bee is crouching and prodding at a snail nearby while Tsembi shouts at her to give it a rest, he’s only little, give it a rest
At the turnstile she counts heads and shoves the handful of coins in
They throw their towels down onto the brown grass and the kids strip their clothes off and fight over swimming costumes
She slathers sun cream on arms and legs and tries to stop Bee from falling in
Douglas examines his willy with his legs in the air and cries when a fat bee stings him on his round little belly
She scoops him up in one arm and gives him a sandwich

The older children are wading into the shallow end and lifting the water up in their hands and throwing it at one another, and Leo is dunking his head beneath the surface, where it must be good and quiet
Ori is leaping from the side over and over again, the force of her body leaving an after‑star‑shape in the air
Ruth gives Bee a sandwich too and puts on her own costume
It is one of JP’s and cuts in around the shoulders

Her mind is a rushing thing, trying to keep everyone in sight, tallying up who has sun cream on, thinking about what needs doing that day back at the house, thinking about the wood lice that have infested the room where she, JP, Leo, Nora and Ori sleep, which seem to dig their way up through the floors
There is a leak coming through the roof when it rains and sewage down the wall in the concrete yard whenever anyone upstairs flushes the chain
JP was beside her on the blow‑up mattress and Leo and Nora were sprawled across the single beds, but when she looked again, Ori was not there
There was noise from the rooms above, which are rented out separately by students whom they almost never see, only hear
She had a sudden damp nightmare vision of Ori being spirited away or, rather, having never existed—she had never had a child

title: Welcome to the Era of Second-Screen Reading
excerpt: T hree thousand two hundred pages into Sarah J
body: T hree thousand two hundred pages into Sarah J
Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses series, I became very worried that I was missing something
I had read close to the page-count equivalent of Proust’s In Search of Lost Time , but by the end of the latest entry, A Court of Splintered Harmony , published last month, my head was spinning
All of the human queens were a muddle for me

Had I missed the locations of the three kingdoms with which our heroes were locked in a diplomatic stalemate? And who, exactly, was Bryce? Half of all Americans don’t finish even a book a year, and yet millions of people in this country have read the six ACOTAR novels
Over the past few months, as I embarked on the task of joining those millions, I found the series everywhere

Readers wanted to talk about it with me while white-water tubing in West Virginia; a high-school classmate dissected the plot via Instagram DM; the books came up at a friend’s house party and on a bachelorette trip

These friends and acquaintances, along with so many others, have read—or will soon finish— Splintered Harmony (and then await, in January, its forthcoming 896-page sequel, A Court of Forgotten Melody )
Surely, they aren’t as baffled by its swirl of plots and characters as I am

I’d set out on my journey through Prythian, Maas’s faerie realm, in hopes of understanding what made both earnest fans of genre fiction and women I had never considered bookish tear through so many pages in so many numbers
I consider myself a close and deliberate reader, and I’m not a snob—I enjoy both fantasy and romance

But all of my attempts to decipher the Maas magic seemed to fail: I’d either work myself up about the incoherence of her society’s rules and history, or I’d bounce off the text altogether, like a kid sliding down the smooth sides of an inflatable castle
That feeling frustrated me—until I realized I’d been reading it wrong
There are, undeniably, ACOTAR obsessives—people who know all about the history of Prythian and its courts, and who instantly recognized Bryce Quinlan, a crossover character from another Maas series
Plenty of fans read, analyze, highlight, and speculate on social media

But it seems unlikely that they could make up the majority of the people who bought 1.7 million copies of Splintered Harmony on the day of its release. [ Read: Don’t call them trash ] After I’d finished submerging myself in reams of ACOTAR , a different possibility came to mind: The average fan isn’t overly concerned with all these details—and that’s fine, because these books don’t need you to be
They encourage a new kind of reading, more akin to the Marvel Cinematic Universe than the best-selling worlds of J
Rowling, James Patterson, or Jackie Collins
They travel differently too: A core of Easter-egg hunters spreads the word to casual fans, who are drawn mostly to the spectacle
Maas’s books aren’t the first blockbusters designed to be flipped through passively, maybe on a beach or with your phone in hand, but the bifurcated readership is noteworthy
You can choose to lock in, or you can sit back and offer up nothing but your presence and passive delight
The second path, I would argue, is more rewarding
W e might be at the end of reading, as my colleague Rose Horowitch reported pessimistically in July
The desire—and ability—to consume books for pleasure is dwindling, by many metrics, and scientists warn that phones are rotting our attention spans
In this environment, the success of ACOTAR , a doorstop series with no film or television adaptation, might seem puzzling

It follows a human girl, Feyre, who gets caught up in the drama of the faerie world next door; she initially falls in love with one hunky Fae man, only to leave him and marry the smoldering bad boy she’d told him not to worry about
By the time of Splintered Harmony , Feyre and her two sisters have all been turned into faeries and live in the magical realm
She’s the High Lady of the Night Court alongside her mate, Rhysand, and they have a six-month-old baby
There are ancient rites, magical weapons, and prophetic seers
And there is a fair amount of sex: Since 2015, when the first book was released, the series has become the poster child for the romantasy boom
A surface-level way to understand these books’ popularity is to assume that readers are there for the smut; having grown up with fantasy, they’re ready—and eager—for a mature version of it
That’s certainly a selling point, but compared with similar entries in the genre, Maas’s books are fairly tame, with a very high plot-to-horniness ratio

And many of the fans I’ve met will admit, cheerfully, that the sex isn’t all that earthshaking. (The sex scenes are also where Maas shows off some of her most awkward tics; she insists, for example, on calling a character’s orgasm their “release.”) Maas, I think, is offering readers something different—a genuinely epic story that goes down like a Netflix binge, one you can half pay attention to and still robustly enjoy
Like the MCU, it sets off enough fireworks to hook distracted readers who couldn’t care less who Bryce is, but unlike, say, Patterson, ACOTAR isn’t propelled by the question of what will happen next

Instead, Maas offers a kind of second-screen reading: rich in detail but low on crucial narration that cannot be missed. [ Read: The rise of must-read TV ] I don’t mean to imply that she’s making scenes skippable on purpose

Everything Maas has written suggests that she cares about building and expanding her magical realms, that she’s thought about the origins of Prythian’s kingdoms, and that she intends to resolve some of the series’ mysteries
Nor do I believe that she’s being asked by her editors to whittle down or simplify her lore to boost sales (in fact, the sprawling faerie world just keeps expanding, to the series’ detriment)
It’s just that her building blocks aren’t all load-bearing, in part because they seem interchangeable

Men will “growl” their lines of dialogue many times in the series, and a reader’s eyes will barely register it—except at clearly signposted moments (as when Rhysand growls at Feyre, “Don’t bother buttoning up that nightgown”)
Splintered Harmony frequently mentions Rask, Montesere, and Vallahan, three kingdoms our heroes hope to recruit to their war effort

title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
excerpt: Record-low hydropower in the Southwest: The US Southwest generated 28% less hydropower than its 10-year average this past spring and summer, driven by a 27-year
body: Record-low hydropower in the Southwest: The US Southwest generated 28% less hydropower than its 10-year average this past spring and summer, driven by a 27-year drought
That has pushed the region's two largest reservoirs, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, dangerously close to the minimum levels needed to generate electricity

Climate change is making things worse: Rising temperatures mean less snow to fill reservoirs, more droughts, and increasingly unpredictable precipitation, a combination that can make hydropower less reliable
The emissions ripple effect: When hydropower falters, the consequences extend beyond the power grid

A global shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for roughly 40% of the 1.1% rise in energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions in 2023, according to the International Energy Agency. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148742" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration
Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs
The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand
But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases
Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River

And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.  Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants
At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant
The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September

Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.  Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years

Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.  The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.  But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study

Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.  Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA
El Niño could provide some temporary relief
Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US
Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low
But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions
Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher
In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally
A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

title: While the term ‘Friendsgiving’ is new, the tradition has been around for decades – found family and experimental freedom make this holiday special
url:
<title>While the term ‘Friendsgiving’ is new, the tradition has been around for decades – found family and experimental freedom make this holiday special</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771753/original/file-20261112-64-6wqgf2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">While &quot;Friendsgiving&quot; is a modern term, people have been gathering with friends for centuries. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/top-down-view-of-holiday-feast-royalty-free-image/2220704403?phrase=thanksgiving&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Alina Rudya/Bell Collective/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud. </p>

<p>I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape. </p>

<p>While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.</p>

<p>My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.</p>

<p>If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.</p>

<p><a href="https://kchervena.wixsite.com/kirsten-chervenak">As a food studies scholar researching</a> how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that <a href="https://www.npr.org/2025/11/19/nx-s1-5605483/friendsgiving-thanksgiving-friends-history-tips">emerged only in the early 2000s</a> even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering. </p>

<h2>Not your grandma’s dinner party</h2>

<p>Modern American dinner parties still <a href="https://doi.org/https://doi.org/10.59236/ne3159814">have roots in the Victorian era</a>, when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved. </p>

<p>In her book “<a href="https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=p079184">Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality</a>,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p>Within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity. </p>

<p>Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a new recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group.</p>

<h2>A holiday that expands boundaries</h2>

<p>Today, Thanksgiving <a href="https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=p079184">is typically viewed</a> as a family holiday. </p>

<p>For some, this may be the gathering that provides the <a href="https://theconversation.com/an-anthropologist-explains-why-we-love-holiday-rituals-and-traditions-88462">warm, fuzzy holiday feeling</a> many search for. But for others, family holidays are stressful.</p>

<p>A 2023 <a href="https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/apa-holiday-stress-topline-report.pdf">survey of 2,061 adults found that</a> 9 in 10 people reported <a href="https://theconversation.com/parents-and-caregivers-how-to-stop-feeling-like-a-grinch-and-be-more-present-with-your-kids-this-holiday-season-240188">experiencing stress</a> around money, lost loved ones, <a href="https://theconversation.com/constructive-arguing-can-help-keep-the-peace-at-your-thanksgiving-table-150429">familial conflict</a> or other expectations during the holidays.</p>

<p>As Friendsgiving isn’t an established holiday, participation is difficult to capture. But of 1,000 people surveyed in 2024, <a href="https://www.statista.com/chart/28817/thanksgiving-plans-gcs/">20% said they planned to celebrate Friendsgiving</a>.</p>

<p>A Friendsgiving is the opposite of established kin-keeping traditions. It gives the opportunity to gather with <a href="https://www.indiependent.co.uk/a-deep-dive-into-tropes-found-family/">found family</a>, and while the reason for gathering is established, the form is malleable. </p>

<p>Many people choose a potluck-style as a way of sharing the burden for what can be a labor-intensive meal. Others choose to do away entirely with what is considered the “traditional” meal and showcase foods from their own culture or a cuisine they enjoy. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As a parody of a holiday, Friendsgiving gives participants permission to make the holiday their own and be as playful as they wish. So, if I burn my miso butter corn casserole, no one will be disappointed, because they’ve never tasted it before anyway.</p>

<h2>How to host a successful Friendsgiving</h2>

<p>While playing with form and bucking traditional structure can be rewarding, there are some things you may want to keep in mind to have a successful Friendsgiving. </p>

<p>In her book “<a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/319055/the-art-of-gathering-by-priya-parker/">The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why it Matters</a>,” author Priya Parker advises anyone planning a gathering to be specific about purpose. This will help decide the form of the event and whom to invite. </p>

<p>Is this a casual gathering with friends? Is fellowship or food more important? Are you hoping to try a recipe your family would never approve? Be specific about your own expectations before you start planning. </p>

<p>The Emily Post Institute, which promotes etiquette and offers resources for a variety of social situations, <a href="https://emilypost.com/advice/party-etiquette-tips-for-hosts-and-guests">recommends being flexible</a> with the menu. This is especially important for a potluck-style gathering. As a host, you may want to assign dishes to guests to ensure a balanced meal without eight desserts. If you have the gumption, however, you can throw caution to the wind and see what happens. </p>

<p>It is also important to keep dietary restrictions in mind to make sure everyone feels included and has something to eat. </p>

<p>Make a plan for heating or reheating. The oven is prime real estate during Thanksgiving. You may want to tell guests to bring their dish already cooked to avoid playing oven Tetris. </p>

<p>Finally, tell guests to bring Tupperware. There will be leftovers, and I have found that nothing is better than creating a second plate to take home and heat up the next day.</p>

<title>Jensen Huang scandal illustrates why human nature is cybersecurity’s weakest link</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772554/original/file-20261117-64-vnkx1f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=879%2C1421%2C3310%2C2206&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Huang is hardly the first powerful person to lower their defenses.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-delivers-the-keynote-address-during-news-photo/2205790189">Justin Sullivan/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/business/business-news/what-is-nvidia-what-do-they-make-ai-artificial-intelligence-rcna140171">whose growth has been propelled</a> by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature.</p>

<p>Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/technology/alice-huang-megaspeed-nvidia-jensen-huang.html">whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China</a>. The company <a href="https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/statement-from-nvidia-board-of-directors">says no secrets were leaked</a>.</p>

<p>In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “<a href="https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-introductory-computer-science/the-art-of-deception-controlling-the-human-element-of-security-p-9780764542800">human factor is truly security’s weakest link</a>.”</p>

<p>Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, <a href="https://apnews.com/article/italy-ukraine-war-fatigue-pranksters-russian-meloni-9adb35302825293e81050923fb2b90f9">Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni</a> spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director <a href="https://www.npr.org/2015/03/03/390484860/petraeus-agrees-to-plead-guilty-to-improperly-handling-classified-information">David Petraeus</a> gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information.</p>

<p>These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment? </p>

<p>Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. <a href="https://www.ilr.cornell.edu/people/vanessa-bohns">As a social psychologist</a> who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting – and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information or take risks.</p>

<h2>The comfort of a human voice</h2>

<p>Mitnick has been called “<a href="https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/hackers/whoare/testimony.html">the most notorious hacker of all time</a>.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets. </p>

<p>He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him.</p>

<p>In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617713798">Studies show</a> that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more  capable and relatable. Interactions via <a href="https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2020-64844-001">phone, video chat and voice chat</a> also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email. </p>

<p>Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/19485506211063259">In a study</a> I conducted with social psychologist <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=tsxBf8oAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Mahdi Roghanizad</a>, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many “yes” responses over the phone as they did by email.</p>

<p>When it comes to obtaining company secrets or <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/trump-administration-moves-to-block-china-from-indirect-access-to-american-ai-tech">circumventing export laws</a>, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have.</p>

<h2>The Midas touch</h2>

<p>Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167284104003">on tipping behavior</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00987054">acquiescence</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610369493">risk-taking</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167284104003">In a famous 1984 study</a>, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(77)90044-0">classic psychology study</a>, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change.</p>

<p>The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets. </p>

<p>Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610369493">In a 2010 study</a>, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A close-up of a woman's index finger, which has its nail painted grey-blue, touching black leather clothing." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772542/original/file-20261117-64-aif1m4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C300%2C5760%2C3240&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772542/original/file-20261117-64-aif1m4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772542/original/file-20261117-64-aif1m4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772542/original/file-20261117-64-aif1m4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772542/original/file-20261117-64-aif1m4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772542/original/file-20261117-64-aif1m4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772542/original/file-20261117-64-aif1m4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A reassuring touch can make people more generous and more willing to take risks.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/womens-hands-with-a-stylish-manicure-royalty-free-image/482155886?phrase=hand%20touching%20shoulder%20leather%20jacket&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">abezikus/iStock via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The power of face-to-face</h2>

<p>Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/001872676501800105">Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment</a>, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about.</p>

<p>In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2015/01/rethinking-one-of-psychologys-most-infamous-experiments/384913/">Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings</a>, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face. </p>

<p>In <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2016.10.002">one study</a>, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/19485506211063259">another study</a>, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call.</p>

<p>Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296763/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Huang is hardly the first powerful person to lower their defenses
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images The end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony

The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature
Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China

In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “ human factor is truly security’s weakest link .” Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses
In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation
In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information

These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment? Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings
As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive
Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting – and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information or take risks

The comfort of a human voice Mitnick has been called “ the most notorious hacker of all time .” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola
He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets
He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague
The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him
In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice
Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable
Interactions via phone, video chat and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email
Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text
In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad , participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels
They received about twice as many “yes” responses over the phone as they did by email
When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws , a human voice may be all you need
The Midas touch Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior , acquiescence and risk-taking
In a famous 1984 study , a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips
In another classic psychology study , female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone
When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change
The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity
That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets
Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks
In a 2010 study , participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder

A reassuring touch can make people more generous and more willing to take risks. abezikus/iStock via Getty Images The power of face-to-face Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment , illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about
In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant
The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks
Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting
In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone
In this version, only 22.5% went that far

Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings , my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face
In one study , participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email
In another study , in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call
Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security
But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you

<title>Fighting in Yemen has made crossing the Bab el-Mandeb even more dangerous – jeopardizing aid and refuge for millions</title>
    <content type="html"><p>In recent days, Iran-backed Houthi forces have <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/16/houthis-edge-closer-to-aden-as-yemeni-forces-pull-out-of-bab-al-mandeb">gained greater control</a> of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital hub of trade, travel and migration between the Middle East and Africa. </p>

<p>The partial closing of the <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/30/iran-war-strait-hormuz-gulf-oil-fuel.html">Strait of Hormuz</a> as part of the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/iran/">war in Iran</a> – and escalating conflicts in <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/world/middleeast/yemen-houthis-saudi-arabia-sanaa-taiz.html">Yemen</a>, <a href="https://apnews.com/article/ethiopia-tigray-eritrea-abiy-ahmed-nile-18294adeefc435193ab569ddb9aa3d60">Ethiopia and Eritrea</a> – had already brought this narrow waterway into new global prominence. Control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains critical to military operations and commodity markets throughout the region. </p>

<p>However, the Bab el-Mandeb’s <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/why-is-bab-el-mandeb-strait-so-important-2026-09-10/">strategic geopolitical</a> and <a href="https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2026-09-27/new-flash-point-in-iran-war-narrow-strait-called-gate-of-tears">commercial shipping</a> importance has largely overshadowed its role as a critical humanitarian corridor.</p>

<p>Bab el-Mandeb means “gate of lamentation” or, more poetically, “gate of tears” in Arabic. It remains one of the <a href="https://storyteller.iom.int/gallery/understanding-migration-along-eastern-route-through-djibouti">most dangerous migration passages</a> in the world. Last year, <a href="https://mixedmigration.org/publications/mmr/2026/bab-el-mandeb-yemenis-flee-migrants-arrive/">more than 900 people died or went missing</a> trying to cross. In October 2026, a <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168573">boat capsized</a> off the coast of Djibouti carrying nearly 300 people, many of whom were escaping violence and persecution. </p>

<p>Meanwhile, <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168706">millions of people in Yemen</a> and throughout the <a href="https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/eastern-africa-el-nino-status-and-humanitarian-impacts-september-2026">Horn of Africa</a> face destitution or death without access to lifesaving deliveries of humanitarian relief supplies shipped through the strait.</p>

<p>Our years of research and forthcoming book “<a href="https://iupress.org/9780253077745/refugees-without-refuge/">Refugees Without Refuge</a>” demonstrate how the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is key to the lives of millions of people throughout the region seeking safety, opportunity and humanitarian assistance. Protecting the safe movement of people and goods through the strait is key to averting future tragedies.   </p>

<h2>A corridor for travel, trade and escape</h2>

<p>Located at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, between the arid coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen, the <a href="https://www.straitstimes.com/world/middle-east/explainer-why-is-the-bab-el-mandeb-strait-so-important">Bab el-Mandeb Strait</a> connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez Canal. On a clear day along the wide beaches and mangrove forests on the coast of Djibouti, you can see the sandy hills on the shores of Yemen, only about 20 to 30 miles away. On starry nights, the scattered lights of coastal towns twinkle across the waters. </p>

<p><iframe id="y0KKy" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/y0KKy/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait"></iframe></p>

<p>For centuries, passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has been vital to <a href="https://academic.oup.com/cairo-scholarship-online/book/18498">global trade in salt, spices, coffee, livestock</a> and other goods. Religious <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/life-of-the-red-sea-dhow-9781786734877/">pilgrims, travelers, migrants and traders</a> have long used the strait for relatively easy transport between continents. </p>

<p>Today, people crossing the strait are also escaping <a href="https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-feature/2025/04/23/ethiopia-frustrated-youth-south-south-migration-africa">poverty, war, political persecution, disasters</a> and <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-modern-african-studies/article/building-ones-own-house-power-and-escape-for-ethiopian-women-through-international-migration/69BC32D1B25D029D04046955A316AEA6">gender-based violence</a>. </p>

<p>Hot, tired, financially depleted and frequently sick or injured, refugees and migrants traverse the Bab el-Mandeb at all hours. </p>

<p>Most negotiate passage across the strait on derelict boats with “delalas” – facilitators, brokers or smugglers – in the shadows of coast guard and police patrols and outside United Nations and governmental migration controls.</p>

<p>The numbers of people crossing the strait are difficult to estimate. Between January and August 2026, the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration recorded <a href="https://dtm.iom.int/reports/yemen-flow-monitoring-registry-dashboard-incoming-and-outgoing-migrants-august-2026?close=true">122,258 arrivals</a> to Yemen from the Horn of Africa – even more than had crossed by that time in 2025. Most of these migrants were from Ethiopia, and most traveled without passports or visas. </p>

<p>Since August, displacement and insecurity throughout the region has worsened, making accurate figures for the numbers of people migrating and the numbers of people dying trying to cross impossible to estimate. </p>

<h2>A lifeline for those escaping conflict</h2>

<p>Despite the dangers of this crossing, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains an economic lifeline for millions of people living in Ethiopia, Kenya, Somaliland, Somalia and elsewhere who rely on commercial goods imported from the Middle East and Asia. However, the <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/22/g-s1-144261/yemen-houthis-saudi-iran-humanitarian-crisis">Houthi forces in charge of increasing swaths of southwestern Yemen</a> now control most critical ports and islands in the strait, increasing the risks and costs of transit and trade. </p>

<p>The strait has <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/22/g-s1-144261/yemen-houthis-saudi-iran-humanitarian-crisis">either been closed</a> or has become a bottleneck, allowing only <a href="https://straitinsider.com/bab-el-mandeb/current-status/">limited shipping traffic since September 2026</a>. Many cargo ships have been delayed or rerouted, causing businesses in fragile regional economies to <a href="https://africacenter.org/spotlight/2026-houthi-red-sea-threats/">pass higher transport and fuel costs</a> on to their customers. </p>

<p>The economic effects of costly and delayed shipping and trade through the strait has compounded the broader effects of increased violence and displacement throughout the region. In front of the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 26, 2026, Djibouti foreign minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar <a href="https://webtv.un.org/en/asset/k1s/k1scjbpkdi#edit-terms--uMcLDWgYS60">expressed “grave concern”</a> about the sudden influx of Yemeni refugees putting a strain on underresourced coastal towns and refugee camps. The United Nations relief agency, UNHCR, is reporting an <a href="https://www.londondaily.news/unhcr-reports-confirmed-cholera-outbreak-at-markazi-camp/">outbreak of cholera</a> in the Markazi refugee camp, the primary home to thousands of Yemenis who have fled across the strait into northern Djibouti.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772047/original/file-20261115-64-kjic24.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two men in uniform stand next to a boat" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772047/original/file-20261115-64-kjic24.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772047/original/file-20261115-64-kjic24.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772047/original/file-20261115-64-kjic24.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772047/original/file-20261115-64-kjic24.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772047/original/file-20261115-64-kjic24.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772047/original/file-20261115-64-kjic24.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772047/original/file-20261115-64-kjic24.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
