              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/members-of-the-djiboutian-coast-guard-inspect-boats-seized-news-photo/2273084825?phrase=Djibouti%20refugees%20boat&amp;adppopup=true">Luis Tato/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>On top of that, the <a href="https://www.crisisgroup.org/pod/africa/ethiopia/back-war-ethiopia-0?utm_source=substack&amp;utm_medium=email">potential for a return to civil war in Ethiopia</a>, and the potential <a href="https://newlinesmag.com/podcast/why-ethiopia-is-at-war-once-again/?utm_source=substack&amp;utm_medium=email">involvement of Eritrea</a> in regional conflicts, may increase population displacement and further disrupt economic markets on both sides of the strait. </p>

<p>As each of these conflicts unfolds, additional pressure will likely be put on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It provides the only feasible passage for many people seeking safety and opportunity abroad. </p>

<h2>A humanitarian corridor</h2>

<p>Keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open and safe is also vital for the delivery of humanitarian aid. Like challenges of commercial shipping, the <a href="https://www.wfp.org/stories/what-do-disruptions-major-trade-routes-mean-food-security">maritime transit of relief supplies</a>, including food and medicine, has been undermined by security risks, shipping delays and the rising costs of food and fuel. </p>

<p>UNICEF’s <a href="https://www.unicefusa.org/stories/climate-shocks-and-aid-cuts-deepen-somalias-hunger-crisis">latest situation report for Somalia</a>, published in August 2026, estimates that nearly 5 million people there are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. At least another 5.5 million people in Ethiopia <a href="https://www.unocha.org/news/todays-top-news-ethiopia-democratic-republic-congo-yemen-occupied-palestinian-territory-haiti">are also in need</a>, due to the effects of conflict combined with below-average rainfall linked to El Niño. </p>

<p>In Yemen, an estimated <a href="https://reliefweb.int/report/yemen/yemen-situation-unhcr-emergency-update-external-update-7-10-november-2026">321,000 people have been displaced</a> since Aug. 1, 2026, and <a href="https://www.oxfam.org.au/blog/yemen-water-crisis/">ongoing water scarcity combined with conflict</a> has left 17 million people without access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene services. As casualties mount and cholera spreads, <a href="https://www.emro.who.int/images/stories/yemen/Yemen-Conflict-Escalation-Situation-Report-05.pdf">hospitals have struggled</a> to obtain essential supplies. </p>

<p>The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of all of these crises. It remains a vital human and humanitarian corridor for millions of people needing refuge and relief. It is a lifeline as much as a geopolitical and economic linchpin. </p>

<p>Ensuring the safe passage of people and supplies of humanitarian relief through these waters is necessary to save lives and protect precarious livelihoods throughout the region.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295106/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Why Americans are losing confidence in public education

<title>Why Americans are losing confidence in public education</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772264/original/file-20261116-64-3pmlrp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5621%2C3747&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Lack of trust in schools can have various ripple effects, including teacher burnout.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/kindergarten-classroom-royalty-free-image/1130969060?phrase=public%20schools&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Mint Images/Getty Images </a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Americans’ satisfaction with public education has fallen to its lowest level since 1999.</p>

<p>Less than a third of Americans were satisfied with public education in 2026, compared with more than half who felt this way in 2019 and 1999, according to a <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/714017/satisfaction-education-hits-new-low.aspx">September 2026 Gallup poll</a>. </p>

<p>Parents typically give their own children’s education higher marks, reflecting a broader tendency to view familiar local institutions more favorably. But parents’ satisfaction with their children’s schools has also reached a record low: 66% of parents reported being satisfied in 2026, down from 83% in 1999. </p>

<p>Declining test scores, <a href="https://www.nspra.org/Portals/0/NSPRA_MisInfoReport_Release.pdf?ver=x3VghH-3kAJeAFC_cplb1w%3d%3d">misinformation about public education</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/00317217231156223">culture war issues</a> and a general <a href="https://kappanonline.org/what-do-adults-know-about-public-education/">lack of knowledge about what K-12 schools are teaching</a> have all contributed to this drop in satisfaction. </p>

<p>As an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=5EkUDDwAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">education researcher focused on family, school and community relationships</a>, I am concerned that declining satisfaction in public schools could have lasting consequences for students and communities.</p>

<h2>Roots of public education</h2>

<p>Public education in the U.S. was shaped by 19th-century advocates who argued that <a href="https://www.history.com/articles/public-school-america-horace-mann">universal, free and nonsectarian education</a> was essential to the success of a democratic society. </p>

<p>Communities agreed to invest in education because they believed it would benefit everyone, not just families with children, by supporting economic growth and preparing people to work together to solve shared problems.</p>

<p>Sustaining that public investment depends in part on people’s confidence that schools are delivering on these shared goals. </p>

<p>Without that public confidence, schools may struggle to secure the necessary funding and buy-in from the community. Parents may start to doubt that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/edth.12174">their children will be well-educated</a> in public schools. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<h2>The costs of conflict and mistrust</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://news.syr.edu/2025/10/23/the-great-divide-understanding-us-political-polarization/">rise of political polarization</a> in the U.S. has complicated people’s perceptions of education.  </p>

<p><a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2024/02/22/race-and-lgbtq-issues-in-k-12-schools/">Local schools have become flash points</a> in debates over race, gender and what children should learn, and research on school board meetings shows how these conflicts can fuel <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/738771">distrust of school leaders and disrupt how schools are run</a>.</p>

<p>For example, some <a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/DCPD-202000715/pdf/DCPD-202000715.pdf">conservative politicians</a>, <a href="https://www.edweek.org/leadership/litter-boxes-in-schools-how-a-disruptive-and-demeaning-hoax-frustrated-school-leaders/2022/11">media outlets</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.14507/epaa.30.6144">advocacy groups</a> have promoted false claims that schools are using <a href="https://www.edweek.org/leadership/what-is-critical-race-theory-and-why-is-it-under-attack/2021/05">critical race theory</a> – meaning the idea that racism is built into laws, rules and everyday systems in society – to indoctrinate children. </p>

<p>Researchers found that these campaigns have often distorted lessons about racism and efforts to <a href="https://digitalcommons.chapman.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1421&amp;context=education_articles">support students from diverse backgrounds</a>, despite no evidence that critical race theory was widely taught in K-12 schools. </p>

<p>Repeatedly hearing and reading misinformation about public education can make it harder for communities to distinguish reliable, fact-based information from politicized distortions of reality. </p>

<h2>Other carryover effects</h2>

<p>The effects of misinformation can also extend into other areas of school life, including the work that district superintendents and school boards do. </p>

<p>In a 2026 study, my colleagues and I found that 82% of district superintendents felt increasingly concerned about inaccurate information <a href="https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/23328584261489201">circulating about their schools or district decisions</a>. Another 55% reported that school board meetings had become noticeably more contentious over the past few years.</p>

<p>Such conflicts can become expensive. </p>

<p>Disputes over teaching about race and racism, the rights of LGBTQ+ students and access to books cost public schools <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/0161956X.2026.2650968">US$3.2 billion during the 2023-24 school year</a>. This estimate includes legal expenses, security, staff time and the cost of replacing employees who left because of tension or fighting at schools.</p>

<p>Controversy and polarization surrounding public schools can leave teachers feeling that their work is not trusted or valued.</p>

<p>Approximately <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2024/04/04/what-public-k-12-teachers-want-americans-to-know-about-teaching/">47% of teachers</a> believed most Americans trusted teachers little or not at all, according to a 2023 Pew Research Center survey. </p>

<p>Teachers who feel valued <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/results-from-talis-2024_90df6235-en/full-report/the-demands-of-teaching_0e941e2f.html#chapter-d1e11078-37d6897ffa">are more likely to want to stay in the profession</a>. Feeling undervalued may make an <a href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA4404-2.html">already demanding profession less appealing</a>. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Rebuilding confidence in public education</h2>

<p>Regaining people’s trust in public education would involve the difficult task of addressing legitimate public concerns, like students’ <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/13/upshot/test-scores-school-districts-us.html?unlocked_article_code=1.iFA.G_Ub.cXbz5_-EC4R3&amp;smid=url-share">declining test scores</a>. </p>

<p>It would also involve effectively correcting misinformation and diplomatically managing community members’ diverse values and opinions. </p>

<p>Transparency is not just about giving community members more access to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/puar.13603">information about what schools are teaching</a> and how. </p>

<p>I believe it also means that schools should <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2024597118">acknowledge their limitations</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/gove.12021">explain their decisions</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03776-9">respond to community members’ questions</a>.</p>

<p>For example, when parents voice concerns about how race and racism are discussed in classrooms, educators could share teaching materials, explain their learning goals and provide opportunities for questions. </p>

<p>This could help clarify what students are actually learning, correct inaccurate ideas and spark discussions about how these topics should be addressed. These conversations may not result in consensus, but participants gain a clearer understanding of school decisions and the differing views within communities. </p>

<p>School administrators could also connect with families and community members to give them a chance to ask questions, share concerns and brainstorm solutions. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://nepc.colorado.edu/sites/default/files/publications/PM%20Family%20Leadership_0.pdf">Family Leadership Design Collaborative</a>, for example, is a national network led by academics, families, educators and community leaders from across 10 U.S. cities. It works to identify shared educational concerns and draft responses to big educational challenges, including school discipline and racial inequities. </p>

<p>These types of partnerships require a significant commitment. But they offer a chance to give people firsthand opportunities to see how schools can respond to challenges, and to rebuild trust in communities.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293797/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Your gut bacteria helps your body keep track of time, and when you eat influences how much nutrition you get from food</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771742/original/file-20261112-64-h5owk3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=163%2C0%2C1963%2C1308&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Your gut microbes work by 24-hour cycles of day and night.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/intestinal-bacteria-microbiome-royalty-free-image/1458753569">iLexx/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>How your body processes food is significantly influenced by <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-nutr-062122-014528">daily rhythms</a> tied to 24-hour light-dark cycles. In new research published in the scientific journal Cell Host &amp; Microbe, my colleagues <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=5TCNs50AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">and I</a> found that the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2026.09.021">microbes living in your gut are the hidden timekeepers</a> behind this system. </p>

<p>Gut microbes <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2026.09.021">convert dietary signals into molecules</a> that intestinal cells use to synchronize nutrient absorption with feeding times. In mice, this microbe-controlled timing mechanism maximizes the nutrients the mouse’s body takes in and supports growth, especially when food is scarce.</p>

<p>When mice consumed an excess of calories, however, that same system <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2026.09.021">fueled obesity</a>.</p>

<h2>Circadian rhythms</h2>

<p>Because of Earth’s rotation, all animals – including humans – experience <a href="https://theconversation.com/your-body-has-an-internal-clock-that-dictates-when-you-eat-sleep-and-might-have-a-heart-attack-all-based-on-time-of-day-178601">rhythmic shifts of day and night</a>. Your eyes and brain <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11818-019-00215-x">use light signals</a> to coordinate your body’s activities with environmental changes and nutrient availability. Disruption of this temporal alignment, such as through jet lag and night-shift work, is <a href="https://doi.org/10.3109/09540261.2014.911149">associated with a range of health disorders</a>. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Y8ZXOfWUbms?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Your body keeps careful track of time.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>However, light is not the only timekeeper. Your intestines are home to trillions of microbes, called <a href="https://theconversation.com/hangry-bacteria-in-your-gut-microbiome-are-linked-to-chronic-disease-feeding-them-what-they-need-could-lead-to-happier-cells-and-a-healthier-body-199486">the gut microbiome</a>. They play a key role in shaping your physiology, such as metabolism, immunity and even brain activity. </p>

<p>Intriguingly, the microbiome also influences the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/lifemeta/loag003">daily biological rhythms of hosts</a>. My colleagues and I had previously shown that depleting gut bacteria in mice weakens circadian rhythms <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaw3134">in the small intestine</a> and alters them <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2016.11.003">in the colon</a>. These disruptions can affect how well your intestine absorbs and processes fats and other lipids, which may contribute to metabolic disorders such as obesity.</p>

<h2>Microbial timekeepers</h2>

<p>But if gut microbes are never exposed to the light, how do they track time? New research from my team suggests that the answer is feeding time. </p>

<p>We found that the gut microbiota can metabolize <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fchem.2023.1174109">phytate</a> – a food component commonly found in grains, beans, nuts and seeds – and convert it into molecules that activate a specific protein in intestinal cells, subsequently turning on genes involved in transporting nutrients. Conversely, when fasting, a decrease in phytate levels leads to reduced microbial activity and a drop in nutrient absorption. </p>

<p>Through this pathway, microbes <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2026.09.021">align intestinal absorption with when you typically eat</a>, which maximizes the efficiency of nutrient absorption.</p>

<p>Our findings suggest that, like light, food provides time-of-day signals that gut microbes read to determine how your body functions.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771749/original/file-20261112-64-i7h6vb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Microscopy image of clusters of small magenta blobs" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771749/original/file-20261112-64-i7h6vb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771749/original/file-20261112-64-i7h6vb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771749/original/file-20261112-64-i7h6vb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771749/original/file-20261112-64-i7h6vb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771749/original/file-20261112-64-i7h6vb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771749/original/file-20261112-64-i7h6vb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771749/original/file-20261112-64-i7h6vb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption"><em>Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron</em> is a species of bacteria that commonly finds residence in the human gut.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://wwwn.cdc.gov/phil/Details.aspx?pid=2951">V.R. Dowell, Jr./CDC</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Mismatched evolution</h2>

<p>People have <a href="https://theconversation.com/humans-evolved-with-their-microbiomes-like-genes-your-gut-microbes-pass-from-one-generation-to-the-next-190713">co-evolved with their gut microbiota</a> for millennia, implying this microbe-controlled time system carries benefits. </p>

<p>For most of human history, <a href="https://ourworldindata.org/data-insights/global-population-growth-was-fast-but-the-production-of-most-fruits-and-vegetables-increased-even-faster">food was scarce</a>. We hypothesized that this microbial pathway might help people survive and grow under starvation conditions. To test this idea, we fed mice a nutrient-poor diet and gave some of them either a common gut microbe or a molecule it produces that is linked to circadian regulation. We found that undernourished young mice who were given this bacterium or the microbial molecule <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2026.09.021">grew taller and healthier</a> than mice that weren’t, suggesting that this microbial pathway promotes growth and metabolic health when nutrients are limited. </p>

<p>However, many people today have constant access to abundant calories. Rather than nutrient scarcity, obesity has become the dominant dietary challenge. We found that for mice under high-calorie conditions, this microbial pathway <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2026.09.021">promotes excess fat uptake</a> in the body and worsens diet-induced obesity.</p>

<p>Therefore, the same gut microbiome mechanism that helped people thrive can become a liability when it encounters an environment it was never designed for. This is an example of <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-does-your-body-lose-weight-an-obesity-doctor-explains-why-one-size-doesnt-fit-all-in-weight-loss-280022">evolutionary mismatch</a>.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295323/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Gut microbes convert dietary signals into molecules that intestinal cells use to synchronize nutrient absorption with feeding times
In mice, this microbe-controlled timing mechanism maximizes the nutrients the mouse’s body takes in and supports growth, especially when food is scarce
When mice consumed an excess of calories, however, that same system fueled obesity
Circadian rhythms Because of Earth’s rotation, all animals – including humans – experience rhythmic shifts of day and night
Your eyes and brain use light signals to coordinate your body’s activities with environmental changes and nutrient availability
Disruption of this temporal alignment, such as through jet lag and night-shift work, is associated with a range of health disorders
However, light is not the only timekeeper
Your intestines are home to trillions of microbes, called the gut microbiome
They play a key role in shaping your physiology, such as metabolism, immunity and even brain activity
Intriguingly, the microbiome also influences the daily biological rhythms of hosts
My colleagues and I had previously shown that depleting gut bacteria in mice weakens circadian rhythms in the small intestine and alters them in the colon
These disruptions can affect how well your intestine absorbs and processes fats and other lipids, which may contribute to metabolic disorders such as obesity
Microbial timekeepers But if gut microbes are never exposed to the light, how do they track time? New research from my team suggests that the answer is feeding time

We found that the gut microbiota can metabolize phytate – a food component commonly found in grains, beans, nuts and seeds – and convert it into molecules that activate a specific protein in intestinal cells, subsequently turning on genes involved in transporting nutrients
Conversely, when fasting, a decrease in phytate levels leads to reduced microbial activity and a drop in nutrient absorption
Through this pathway, microbes align intestinal absorption with when you typically eat , which maximizes the efficiency of nutrient absorption
Our findings suggest that, like light, food provides time-of-day signals that gut microbes read to determine how your body functions
Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron is a species of bacteria that commonly finds residence in the human gut
Dowell, Jr./CDC Mismatched evolution People have co-evolved with their gut microbiota for millennia, implying this microbe-controlled time system carries benefits
For most of human history, food was scarce
We hypothesized that this microbial pathway might help people survive and grow under starvation conditions
To test this idea, we fed mice a nutrient-poor diet and gave some of them either a common gut microbe or a molecule it produces that is linked to circadian regulation

We found that undernourished young mice who were given this bacterium or the microbial molecule grew taller and healthier than mice that weren’t, suggesting that this microbial pathway promotes growth and metabolic health when nutrients are limited
However, many people today have constant access to abundant calories
Rather than nutrient scarcity, obesity has become the dominant dietary challenge
We found that for mice under high-calorie conditions, this microbial pathway promotes excess fat uptake in the body and worsens diet-induced obesity
Therefore, the same gut microbiome mechanism that helped people thrive can become a liability when it encounters an environment it was never designed for
This is an example of evolutionary mismatch

title: The case for new Democratic leadership
excerpt: Members of Democratic leadership in the House and Senate Democratic walk out of the US Capitol on May 21, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images Afte
body: Members of Democratic leadership in the House and Senate Democratic walk out of the US Capitol on May 21, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images After historic wins in the midterm elections, Democrats now have to decide who will lead their new majorities in the House and the Senate

The House race is expected to be a formality, with current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries as the sole declared candidate for House speaker.  The Senate race, however, is shaping up to be more interesting: In the upper chamber, current minority leader Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge from Maryland Sen

Chris Van Hollen, who argues that Senate Democrats need new leadership to meet the demands of voters who delivered them a majority. “The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual,” Van Hollen said . “And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”  Van Hollen is also the favored candidate of the party’s progressive faction, many members of which have soured on Schumer
Corbin Trent, a former communications director for Rep

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and the founder of the super PAC A Fight Worth Having, is one of those: He tells Today, Explained that Schumer’s and Jeffries’s style of leadership is ill-suited for this moment, and he wants to see new Democratic leaders in both chambers
He also argues that Democrats should embrace a more proactive style of governing that harkens back to the New Deal era

Trent spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about who he wants to see lead the Democrats instead, why consensus-building is not enough, and why now is the right time to have this fight.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify

Who do you think should be leading Democrats in the House and Senate in the new year? I think that this moment calls for some sort of leadership that shows that we have a plan, an agenda, and a vision that’s capable of taking on and meeting this moment
It’s not Chuck Schumer.  I know that’s the way we do things in the House, that’s the way we do things in the Senate
But look at the popularity of both of those institutions and then think to yourself, maybe we should do things a little differently
Why not Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer? Hakeem Jeffries has proven either one of two things

Either he’s incapable of wrangling the caucus, or his priorities are very different than the Democratic Party and the independent voters that voted for the Democrats in this election.  What I mean by that is we’ve had three shots at stripping war powers away from Donald Trump vis-a-vis Iran
And, oh, lo and behold, one, two, three Democrats defected He is not supporting an arms embargo to Israel
He’s not a guy who is representing the will of the people writ large
He is very much the establishment Democrat that I think led to Donald Trump being elected twice.  Chuck Schumer is a man with a strongly worded letter in his back pocket
He’s the man that wants to pick up a couple of voters in rural Pennsylvania that are Republicans

Neither of them have a vision for building a Democratic supermajority that is akin to the one that was built around the New Deal.  I think that this moment is very similar to that moment in that it is rife with opportunity
People are hopeful, people are ready for change, but the problem with hope is that when it’s dashed, it calcifies and it becomes resentment and anger
And Democrats seem to miss that every time
I can remember how inspired I was by Barack Obama during his first presidential campaign — so inspired that I got involved in politics
I went to an event in Asheville to watch him speak
I started raising money for him on his portal, and I had a watch party
It was not my thing, but he inspired me to do all this stuff
And then several months later, what I’m hearing is a very different thing as a president than as a candidate
So we can’t keep missing these opportunities, in my mind
Why do Jeffries and Schumer seem so confident in this moment? Schumer has a challenger, Chris Van Hollen
Hakeem kind of has one in Ayanna Pressley, but they don’t seem very worried that their positions might be in jeopardy right now
How come? Because that’s just not the way things are done in the House, and they I think have faith that things will continue being done the way they are
Momentum, norms, all of these things point to them not having any real problem getting their leadership taken away
And then famously AOC spanked his little bottom in 2018 , and now he’s a consultant instead of a congressman
Now we’d be having a very different conversation, because he was the one that was in line to be the next speaker of the House
How come? What’s your reaction to that? I mean, is she backing Jeffries? She’s doing this weird little thread-the-needle: “He’s the only one
What can we do?”  But that’s the exact kind of thinking that you’re saying Democrats should rebuff
And interestingly, the most important thing to learn from Nancy Pelosi in my mind is that power is not given, it is taken
Power is not something that people give you
It is something that you take and then utilize.  The fact is that [the Congressional Progressive Caucus] has 99 members, and it is going to have more

The fact is that these members have the capacity to generate more media than most.  They can either take this moment to build power for the American people that ends up building a super-majoritarian Democratic Party, one that can make the Republican Party small enough to drown in a bathtub , or they can try to do business as usual, work with Hakeem, work with Schumer, try to extract some concessions, which they will not give.  Because like you say, they have no fear
They respond to threats and fear, fear of losing their job
Help us understand why someone like AOC doesn’t want this job

title: When do we start worrying about all these outages?
excerpt: Have you tried to take a flight in the last week? What about check your email , your bank balance , your Apple account ? (Or, for a select few of us, your top-s
body: Have you tried to take a flight in the last week? What about check your email , your bank balance , your Apple account ? (Or, for a select few of us, your top-secret internal spy agency network ?) If you have, you might have noticed that some or all of those services didn’t work as expected
First, Microsoft’s cloud programs, such as Outlook, went down late last week
Then, all of the planes were grounded on Friday

And this week, we had to deal with the bank outages, a separate United Airlines-specific outage, the Apple outage, and the NSA communications outage.  As of this writing, most of these issues have now been ironed out, at least for the time being, and there’s no indication that any of them were cyberattacks or otherwise malicious

But whatever the reasons, it sure feels like there have been a lot more outages this week and last than in a usual seven-day stretch.  To get to the bottom of it — hopefully before something else shorts out — the Today, Explained team spoke with Lily Hay Newman , a senior writer at WIRED who covers hacking, information security, and digital privacy

She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about why it took Microsoft so long to get Outlook back on its feet, all of the other recent outages we’ve suffered, and whether it’s as unprecedented as it feels in the moment
Plus, she explains how AI is causing a broader “vulnepocalypse” (or “ Vulnageddon ”), even if it’s not specifically the culprit of all of our current outages
Below is an excerpt of Newman’s conversation with Sean, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify

Lily, we spent the first half of the show talking about the issues with our air traffic control systems, but last week, of course, also brought chaos to a lot of people’s inboxes when Outlook was not so good

Microsoft 365, so all of the productivity platforms, had a massive outage and it dragged on for a full day, which is very noticeable when it’s a set of products that are as integrated in everything, as 365 is.  That means you just can’t work, right? This was probably billions of dollars of productivity lost
Yeah, this is the cloud version of Microsoft Office: Outlook, Word, Excel, Copilot, Teams
If that’s your productivity platform, then yeah, you can’t work
Microsoft is so enmeshed in the tech ecosystem, even before all of the cloud platforms, because they’re the Windows maker
They’re in everything.  What happened? Microsoft, a few days later, on Monday, what they were saying was that they had sent out an update
It’s a Windows update, but it’s only really for their infrastructure
It’s not an update in consumer Windows
It’s not something your laptop would’ve gotten, but it has been out and proliferating through their infrastructure for about three months
But it actually had a flaw in it that wasn’t caught by their testing.  At the same time, they say cloud infrastructure is all about managing traffic and managing different regions of data centers

The issue with that three months of proliferation of that update started triggering and that’s why it was such an intractable issue.  At first, I saw it and I thought, okay, it’ll be a few hours, three hours or something, and they’ll fix it
And then, waking up Friday morning, it’s still not fixed
And it’s like, whoa, so something’s really going on.  And so it was the interplay of multiple factors that made it so hard for them to recover, they say.  Okay
Very different situations here between air traffic control and Microsoft 365
However, both kind of have a similar origin story in that they’re about patching systems and upgrading systems
We’ve heard from Sean Duffy, Transportation secretary, that he cannot guarantee what happened on Friday won’t happen again in the near distant future
Have we heard something more reassuring from Microsoft? Microsoft would definitely say, “This isn’t going to happen again

Sometimes problems arise because of cyber attacks or exploitation of vulnerabilities.”  And then it’s kind of like, ‘Well, why weren’t all those systems patched? There was a patch out.’  But a lot of times patching is slower than we would like because the ramifications of a bad patch or an unforeseen consequence of an update can be really severe, and so organizations tend to be very nervous.  But it’s never the last time
These types of outages and failures happen in all technology systems and they will continue to, but people try to learn as much as they can from each incident and make things more and more robust
Maybe a good time to ask you about all of the other breakdowns we’ve been having in our technology and elsewhere over the last few weeks
I mean, people may not have even realized they just lived through something called Black October
What is Black October, beyond Halloween? In October there were a few things going on, including with the widely used web scripting language, PHP

There were these two vulnerabilities in it that researchers were really concerned that if they were exploited, they could cause remote access takeovers of all different websites and all different platforms.  And so there was this big, industry-wide effort to make sure that everybody was patching — a “We have to patch this right away, don’t wait” type of thing
So there’s Black October and then there’s the “vulnepocalypse.” People have been talking about this for maybe about a year now, this idea— Everything’s vulnerable? Right
Or that AI tools— We need a better name for that
I’m just doing air quotes here, heavy air quotes

But this idea that agentic AI and AI models are becoming more and more powerful and adept at finding bugs in software and in helping both researchers and, potentially, attackers figure out how to exploit those vulnerabilities and weaponize them.  There’s this [idea] that cybersecurity is always this cat and mouse — again, I’m doing the air quotes — “cat and mouse game,” or an “arms race” is another phrase that’s often used
And so that in itself is not new, but the idea that AI in the mix just really accelerates it for both sides, and how to manage that dynamic

Then there was this Iranian cyber attack on supermarket fridges or Binance getting hacked for, I don’t know, I think the most money I’ve ever heard about in any kind of hacker heist ever — $6 billion? It was
I thought that we were meant to believe that crypto was unhackable, and here we are getting hacked for $6 billion? I just want everyone to know you can rest easy
The fridge hacks, for example, the vulnerabilities that are being exploited there actually kind of go back numerous years

title: Voyager 1 is about to reach a mind-bending milestone
excerpt: An artist’s rendering of the Voyager approaching Saturn, circa the late 1970s. | Space Fronteirs/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained,&nbsp
body: An artist’s rendering of the Voyager approaching Saturn, circa the late 1970s. | Space Fronteirs/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Shortly after 5 am ET tomorrow morning, while much of the East Coast is still in bed, Voyager 1 will cross a threshold that’s kind of hard to comprehend
The 49-year-old spacecraft will reach a point about 16 billion miles from Earth — the distance that light travels in 24 hours.  Scientists call that unit a light-day
And while it’s not a particularly meaningful scientific measurement, it’s a pretty good opportunity to marvel at how far Voyager has voyaged
The craft first set out in 1977 to explore our solar system’s outer planets, including Jupiter and Saturn

It flew past both planets, snapping photos of their surfaces and making several big discoveries , before reaching interstellar space in 2012.  Today, both Voyager and its sister, Voyager 2, remain part of an active NASA mission measuring the gases and magnetic field outside the Sun’s protective magnetic bubble
Both spacecraft also famously carry identical copies of the so-called Golden Record, which contains images and recordings meant to introduce humanity to passing aliens

That means Voyager isn’t just interesting as a live experiment or a souvenir of America’s 1970s space ambitions — but as an attempted self-portrait of human civilization.  Go a little deeper View Link Voyager will surely lose touch with Earth long before it makes contact with aliens, though

The mission only has a few years left: Its nuclear generators are gradually producing less electricity, which means Voyager is expected to lose the power to fuel its transmitter by 2030 .  But the spacecraft will keep coasting on its momentum, potentially surviving for billions of years with very little around it to wear it down
Which is why, as NASA readied the Voyager missions, it tapped the astronomer Carl Sagan to curate a message for spacefaring aliens

Sagan and his team spent six weeks on the project, which was stored on a gold-plated copper phonograph LP. (In case you’re wondering how aliens will actually play the record, the team provided hieroglyphic instructions that explain where to place the needle and how fast to spin it.)  Sagan’s team decided to leave out images that depicted war, poverty, disease, crime, and religion

The record also reportedly excluded the Beatles’ song “Here Comes the Sun” over a rights-holding dispute, and a photograph of a naked man and pregnant woman because the suits at NASA objected to full-frontal nudes.  But even with those omissions, the team managed to compile an extraordinary collection of images that convey scientific concepts like continental drift and the structure of DNA; depict human anatomy, industry, daily life, and culture; and illustrate the diversity of Earth’s landscapes and animals.  The record also includes letters from former President Jimmy Carter and UN Secretary General Kurt Waldheim, a compilation of sounds from Earth, spoken greetings in more than 50 languages, and 90 minutes of music from around the world

Readers of Liu Cixin’s The Three-Body Problem might distrust this approach. (In it, aliens plan to invade Earth after getting a message from a disgruntled scientist who reveals where the Earth is.) But don’t lose sleep over that possibility
We’ll be long dead before such an invasion could take place: Even the nearest potentially habitable planet is more than four light-years from Earth

And Voyager, as you know, has only traveled one light- day .  One link for later ➨ Try a “bird sit.” It’s basically a nature hike for indoor cats: Find a nice spot outdoors, get comfy, and work on observing the birds that fly past
It’s a great way to appreciate (and get the health and wellness benefits of appreciating) nature without getting your hands dirty

If birds aren’t doing it for you, try plants or insects.  Before you go… Did you know… that TV  kind of does “rot” your brain ? (Sorry, and also: Mom, you were right!) Research has found that heavy TV viewers had less gray matter in midlife
Today’s trivia: Which renowned 13th-century explorer dictated his biography to a prison cellmate? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the European capital that has 343 lakes within its limits
That would be Oslo, which also boasts the highest tree coverage of any capital in Europe.

title: How to be a good-enough home cook
excerpt: Editor’s note, November 17, 2026, 5 pm ET : This story is being republished for the holiday season
body: Editor’s note, November 17, 2026, 5 pm ET : This story is being republished for the holiday season
The running gag among anyone who’s ever tasted a morsel of my cooking is that I must not know what salt is
It’s a fair critique: I somehow manage to overcook and under-season virtually every meal I prepare
I’m clumsy and unconfident with a knife and prefer to prepare most foods in a microwave or Instant Pot.  Whipping up a meal is sometimes a nutritional puzzle
If all you’re working with at the moment are tortillas, frozen broccoli, and canned beans, you (like me) may struggle to conjure up something decent to eat.  Cooking can also feel like a chore
Parents not only have to feed themselves, but send their kids off to school with packed lunches and prepare snacks and dinner after that
One recipe can dirty up a whole sink’s worth of dishes

Just like any other life skill , cooking is one that requires practice. “Eating is such a human thing — that’s the first skill we learn,” says Jess Dang , the founder of the online meal planning service Cook Smarts . “People think if I know how to eat, I must be able to know how to cook too, but they’re totally separate things.” If you weren’t taught the basics of cooking from school or a loved one, you might feel your time in the kitchen is doomed; if you’re already stretched thin financially and time-wise, cooking can feel like a fraught endeavor
However, with a few foundational skills and pantry staples, even the most beginner home chefs can whip up some delicious meals in no time at all
Set some goals in the kitchen While effectively nourishing yourself is an accomplishment in itself, taking on a more active role in the kitchen can be empowering
Maybe your goal is to have a small stable of go-to meals you can pull off without having to look at the recipe (eventually)
Or perhaps you want to improve your knife skills

Rather than give yourself hard and fast milestones to hit, like cooking dinner five nights a week, Dang says to focus on the process of cooking and to lead with curiosity . “Just being curious about the process will help you learn about why things are done the way they are in cooking,” she says. “To me, the goal is each time you’re cooking, try to learn something from that experience, and understand why you’re doing what you’re doing, and that will help you improve over time.” Part of this learning process is accepting the fact that you will make mistakes, but to have fun in spite of them.   Find some recipes before you start Because there are so many meals and types of cuisines to make, cut down on the overwhelm and give yourself some parameters

If you were to dine at a restaurant, what meals would you order? What are your favorite flavors, snacks, textures, proteins, grains, veggies? “It’s just letting your natural inclinations of what you want to eat guide what you want to cook,” Dang says
If your kids are picky eaters, ask them what they don’t like about certain foods, suggests Ben Leonard , a resident chef and instructor at Sur La Table
That way you can get a better idea of what it is that turns them off — the dryness of baked chicken, the bitterness of kale — and adjust accordingly
Then, find some recipes that incorporate your favorite ingredients, flavors, and dishes

The internet is brimming with free recipes, but experts recommend sticking to tried-and-true instructions created by chefs or publications with test kitchens: Food & Wine , New York Times (you’ll need a subscription for this), Allrecipes , Bon Appétit (which can sometimes not be super beginner-friendly), Molly Stevens , Gaby Dalkin , and Nik Sharma

As far as easy-to-parse cookbooks, Jen Nurse, the co-founder of San Francisco-based cooking school The Civic Kitchen , suggests Salt Fat Acid Heat by Samin Nosrat. “I think that’s a great book for beginners because it explains why you do things and how to taste,” she says

Cookbook author and Vox contributor Leanne Brown dedicated a whole cookbook ( available in PDF form for free! ) to low-cost recipes.   Kitchen equipment you’ll need Splurging on a stand mixer might be tempting, but beginners do not need fancy kitchen tools

If there’s one item worth spending a little more on, experts are unanimous on the importance of a decent knife . “You can get a great basic knife for not too much money,” Nurse says. “A lot of people are shocked to hear knife stores expect you to try the knife before you buy it

You want to know it doesn’t dig into your finger in a weird place.” You can get a mid-tier beginner-friendly chef’s knife for anywhere from $40 to $ 150 or peruse Facebook Marketplace, Buy Nothing groups, and Craigslist for second-hand knives
If any of your friends are more advanced in the kitchen, ask them if they have a spare knife they can gift you
Just remember to keep your blade sharp. (You can take it to a professional knife sharpener once a year to get sharpened or sharpen it at home

Just be aware that a honing rod does not sharpen a knife , it only helps keep an already sharp knife sharp.) A dull knife can be dangerous because it’s difficult to pierce your food, forcing you to press down harder, potentially allowing for more accidents
However, don’t overlook pre-made, seasoned, or chopped store-bought items like fruits, veggies, meats, salad kits, sauces, macaroni and cheese, and doughs

Not only are these items huge time-savers, pre-chopped frozen and fresh produce can be extremely helpful for folks with disabilities and other physical barriers that make chopping difficult. “Frozen bell pepper, frozen onion, frozen celery: get it and use it,” says Danni Rose , a cookbook author and food personality. “I do it all the time and my food still tastes good and seasoned.” Along with your knife, you’ll need a cutting board (you can get a pair for less than $2 at Ikea ), a beginner pots and pan set with two saucepans (one larger for pasta and soup), and two skillets
Baking sheets are also good to have for roasting just about any veggie or protein, Nurse says

Again, buying these items secondhand online or at a yard sale can help lower the cost.  As for the spices in your cabinet, Rose is a staunch supporter of garlic powder, onion powder, Kosher salt, and black pepper . “I can go down to Alabama where I’m from and get a fish sandwich on the side of the road that’s literally just been seasoned with those ingredients and it’s battered and fried,” she says, “and it tastes much better than a $150 dish that I see at a Michelin star restaurant.” If you’re feeling a little bolder, you can add some dried parsley, paprika, and Italian and Cajun seasonings to your repertoire, she says.  When it comes to grocery shopping, make sure you have a list of everything you need before stepping foot inside, Dang says, and don’t turn your nose up at discount chain stores like Aldi, Target, and Walmart for cheaper items
Rose likes shopping at specialty stores and markets, like Latin or Asian groceries, to get specific ingredients
Getting started in the kitchen Part of making cooking a pleasurable experience is to make your kitchen an enjoyable place to be
Put on a podcast, album, or audiobook to keep yourself occupied while you’re chopping onions

Or, better yet, enlist the help of your roommates, partner, kids, or parents to make cooking a group effort. “Drink some wine, drink your favorite cocktail, put your favorite music on or your favorite show, and you can watch it while you’re cooking,” Rose says. “Create a good space and environment for you to make good food.” Just as a decent knife is an essential tool, having basic knife skills helps speed the cooking process immensely
Not knowing how to dice an onion, slice a pepper, and chop fresh ginger can turn a 30-minute cooking session into an hour-long one
Dang suggests searching knife skills videos on YouTube for a free primer
If your cutting board doesn’t have a non-slip bottom or grips, put a damp paper towel or kitchen towel under it to make sure the cutting board doesn’t slide around while you’re chopping
Again, if chopping is difficult for you, pre-cut items are available
Once you’ve chosen your recipe, read the instructions in their entirety at least one time

You don’t want to be stirring a simmering pot and feel caught off guard when you realize you need to add a diced zucchini next. “A lot of the prep is going to be hidden in the recipe list,” Nurse says. “Look at that ingredient list

Three cloves of garlic, minced.” AllRecipes and Simply Recipes have great resources defining terms like “minced” (cut into tiny bits) and “sauté” (cook quickly on high heat in a small amount of fat, like olive oil)

title: How Friendsgiving eclipsed Turkey Day
excerpt: Editor’s note, November 17, 2026, 5 pm ET : This story is being republished for the holiday season
body: Editor’s note, November 17, 2026, 5 pm ET : This story is being republished for the holiday season
Sara Reinis, a 26-year-old creative strategist at Vox Media, held her first Friendsgiving last year at her apartment in Brooklyn
Between 30 and 40 people showed up to the potluck, multiple of whom brought dishes from the Whole Foods hot bar

The centerpiece? A cake with icing that read, “Gobble gobble, bitch.” “On the spectrum of ‘typical house party’ to ‘formal Thanksgiving’ it was like, right in the middle,” she says. “The mood was, ‘What if instead of Tostitos, people brought mashed potatoes and pies?’” The evening was a success, clearly — while some people stayed to help clean up, others went out dancing, and Sara even ended up with a collection of new dishware that people neglected to pick up. “It can be very rare in New York to get together and eat home-cooked food,” she adds. “So it felt very intimate and cozy the whole evening — even though it was pretty crowded and rowdy at times.” This weekend, parties like Sara’s will be happening countrywide

Over the past half-decade or so, the week before Thanksgiving has been widely understood as a glorious reprieve before the obligations of actual Thanksgiving, which can range from multi-hour cross-country flights to having to explain who Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is to your great-uncle
By contrast, Friendsgiving season is a time to just hang out with your usual crew and eat slightly more autumnal food than normal
While the concept of celebrating Thanksgiving with friends isn’t exactly new, “Friendsgiving” is

A Merriam-Webster investigation notes that the first usage of the term in print or online was in 2007, in posts on both Usenet and Twitter — and no, it wasn’t because of Friends (even though that would have made a lot of sense)

Friends (the one where Chandler’s in a box). | Paul Drinkwater/NBC/Getty Images" data-portal-copyright="Paul Drinkwater/NBC/Getty Images" /> Instead, Merriam-Webster argues that what shot “Friendsgiving” into the national consciousness was the double-whammy of a 2011 Bailey’s Irish Cream ad campaign and, rather hilariously, an episode of The Real Housewives of New Jersey that aired that same year, in which Teresa hosts a Friendsgiving of her own (this, from the show in which practically every episode someone repeats the idiom “blood is thicker than water”)
In 2013 BuzzFeed declared 17 whole rules for Friendsgiving , and in 2014, the tradition got the Washington Post style section treatment
Back then, the Post described it as something for the lingering “island of misfit toys” who couldn’t or wouldn’t travel the distance to see their families

It also seemed to be particularly popular in cities: “I think DC is the kind of town where there are a lot of people who are from somewhere else, and sometimes friends aren’t able to go home,” one Friendsgiving-goer said
Another offered a different explanation: “I like that I can drink
If I was back with the family, they frown on it
And then you have to drive home.” There are, of course, other rather scientific explanations for the rise of Friendsgiving

Stephanie Coontz, the director of public education at the Council on Contemporary Families, explains that the rising age at which people get married contributes to friendships playing a more significant role in people’s lives

Back in the ’50s and ’60s, she explained, “many marital advice books emphasized how important it was for a wife to make her husband her first priority at all times and not to let girlish friendships interfere with her duties and devotion to her husband.” Meanwhile, because marriage tends to happen much later these days, people place more importance on a network of friends rather than the traditional nuclear family. “Many have also seen what happens when people who haven’t maintained those networks get divorced,” Coontz adds. “So they are also conscious of the need to work on their friendships.” That can translate into spending holidays with friends — either instead of with family, or in addition to it. “For the most part I just think that people have decided to expand their definition of family-like relations,” she says

And there’s an important benefit that comes with Friendsgiving: “No one feels compelled to invite an unsupportive or obnoxious friend the way they often feel pressured to include an unsupportive or obnoxious family member.” A piece in the Atlantic , however, suggests that Friendsgiving is actually a bleak harbinger of millennials’ financial doom

Ashley Fetters writes: Malcolm Harris, meanwhile — the author of the book Kids These Days: Human Capital and the Making of Millennials — sees something darker at work in the “Friendsgiving” phenomenon

Harris thinks affixing the “cutesy” label of Friendsgiving onto a scraped-together, potluck-style event popular among Millennials that will never actually rival the lavish spreads of real Thanksgiving implies approval by the powers that be of Millennial adults’ lower income and lower living standards compared to prior generations. “Friendsgiving,” he says, “is a propaganda weapon used by the ruling class to further their plans for wage stagnation.” Woof! In slightly less bleak (but still pretty bleak) news, the current conversation around Friendsgiving revolves around men, despite presumably being aware of the shitty optics, not offering to help clean up after the meal
A letter-writer to Slate’s Dear Prudence column asked what to do when only the female guests help out with the cleaning while the dudes sit around drinking beer

The answer? Be “cheerfully” direct, and “don’t be afraid to name a conspicuous dynamic.” As for Sara’s 2017 Friendsgiving party, however, the problem wasn’t the dishes: It was wiping the mashed potatoes off the wall the next day.

title: The US has officially lost control of measles
excerpt: A healthcare worker takes down signs at a Maryland vaccine clinic. | Sarah L
body: A healthcare worker takes down signs at a Maryland vaccine clinic. | Sarah L
Voisin/The Washington Post via Getty Images This year, the United States has recorded more measles cases —  5,739 as of Tuesday, November 17 — than in the past 25 years combined
There are active outbreaks in New York , Pennsylvania , and across the Midwest
At least eight people have died with measles infections in the US
None of this is supposed to happen in the 21st century
In 2000, the United States declared that measles had been eliminated

For years, the extremely rare cases the US saw were from people who contracted the virus in another country and brought it back to America; we didn’t have to worry about measles spreading naturally in our communities

The Pan American Health Organization, which works with the countries in the Western Hemisphere on ongoing public health threats as well as emergency response, made it official Monday after the annual meeting of its measles and rubella elimination commission: The United States’ measles elimination status has been revoked
The virus is once again endemic in America
It is an international embarrassment for a country that until very recently was the world’s unquestioned global health leader
And for doctors here in the US who have been practicing for decades, it’s an almost-unthinkable development, putting American lives needlessly at risk

The death of a 7-month-old baby in New York state , who was too young to be vaccinated, has made the consequences of the country’s collective failure hauntingly clear.  “It’s very, very, very surreal,” Dr
Barbara Keber , a family physician in Long Island, New York, told me last week
She’s been practicing medicine for 45 years and is old enough to have gotten measles herself when she was a child

But it was never something she’d had to deal with during her professional career — until now. “When I had it, my sister had it, my best friend had it — that’s how I saw measles,” she said. “Then it disappeared, and I never saw it as a practicing physician until more recently.” The reversal has been dramatic
In 2024, there were just a couple hundred measles cases in the US, nothing out of the ordinary
But last year, there were more than 2,000 measles cases and three deaths, and then both of those figures more than doubled in 2026
This year started with a brutal outbreak in South Carolina, and it is winding down with Pennsylvania in crisis and New York state reporting its first measles death in more than 30 years
It’s impossible to talk about the recent rise of measles without talking about vaccine skepticism
Fears that childhood immunizations cause autism have been growing for years (reminder: they don’t), and the rise of US health secretary Robert F
Kennedy Jr. and a vast network of anti-science activists and politicians has led to widespread distrust in medical science and doctors since the pandemic began
As a result, fewer and fewer American kids are being given their measles shots

Nationwide, the measles vaccination rate is 92.4 percent among kindergarteners, down from 95 percent before the pandemic, which is the threshold public health experts say is necessary to stop the virus from spreading locally
And in some places, the decline has been more severe: In one Texas school district where measles ran wild last year , less than 50 percent of schoolchildren were vaccinated

Over the past two years, I have spoken with doctors working on the front lines of these outbreaks to better understand what it’s like to face measles, often for the first time, and what they hear from their patients in the midst of an outbreak
I’ve taken away three lessons from those conversations, which serve as both an explanation of how we got here and a guide for what to expect as we try to find our way out of this crisis. 1

Small communities can be the kindling for measles outbreaks One clear pattern has emerged across the recent outbreaks: They are often sparked in insular communities where anti-vaccine attitudes — sometimes the result of sincerely held religious reliefs — are widespread
In New York and Pennsylvania right now, for example, measles has taken hold in Amish and Mennonite communities
Last year’s outbreak in Texas started in a Mennonite community as well
A charter school in South Carolina where less than 20 percent of kids were vaccinated against measles was the epicenter of that state’s outbreak
This is a pattern that predates our current measles explosion: When New York endured an isolated outbreak in 2019, it was concentrated in the Hasidic Jewish communities north of New York City

Even in states like New York, where state officials have actually tried to strengthen school vaccine requirements, some parents in these communities have opted to homeschool their kids; they don’t have to follow those mandates

And when they do go out into the world, where more children may be vaccinated on average, they are increasingly likely to encounter another kid who is also unvaccinated as more families overall opt out of those shots

That’s the recipe for these massive outbreaks: A lot of unvaccinated kids in one group get infected and then, as they move around the community, they come into contact with those other kids, who are also unprotected. “These are groups that we have to work very carefully with because they have their religious beliefs

When you speak to them about vaccines, they’re just going to tell you no,” Keber told me. “But the issue there then becomes, well, they might not be being exposed during the school day, but they go and play baseball and they do dance and they do other activities where they’re mixing with other kids.” In some of these communities, skepticism has remained stubbornly high even in the aftermath of an outbreak
But some people do take the threat of measles more seriously after people get sick around them

Keber told me that fear is not really the most effective message for convincing previously skeptical people to get themselves or their children vaccinated; relationship building over time — even if it takes a couple of conversations — is more effective. “We’re not trying to scare people
That doesn’t really help anything,” Keber said. “If they get to trust the physician, that’s the biggest bang for the buck
This is somebody that you trust with the health of yourself and your family.” 2

Doctors are still figuring out how to deal with measles in the wild Measles may be one of the most well-known diseases given its high infectiousness and signature rashes, but because it had been eliminated for so long, many doctors have had only an academic understanding of the virus — at least until these past few years. “Almost no physicians that are currently practicing medicine have ever seen measles,” Keber said

title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers

But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world
These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies

Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech)

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created
They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.  But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI

New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.  On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated
China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead
It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips
DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position

He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China
It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him
The new findings lower Huang’s chances further
What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion

Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.  But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter

The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good
The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers
That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit

title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
excerpt: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them
body: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them
One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t
No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors
For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection
Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses
Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment
We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe
But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built
We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do
We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach
In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit
But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence
Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions

One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry
And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside
Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision
Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior
With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment
Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact
Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed
The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance
Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs
The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI

Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful
Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades

For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations
But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act
The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event
Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk

But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest
Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture

The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark
The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted
It means trust needs a different architecture
Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable
An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription
An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds
An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do
Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter

Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions: What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution
